How to play

Sixty-four hostages are held in four barracks far to the left. Fly out, open the barracks, land beside the hostages so they can climb aboard (16 at most), and fly them home to the base on the right. One barracks is already burning when you start.

Flying

  • ← → tilt and fly. ↑ climbs, ↓ descends; let go to hover. Hold Shift for a gentle push.
  • Land level and slowly. Touch down at full speed and you crash.
  • Hostages only climb in when you are fully landed and still. Don't land on top of them.

Shooting and turning

  • Space or Z fires (in the air only, five shots at a time).
  • Facing sideways, the gun fires ahead: use it on jets and to blow open a barracks.
  • In the painted looks the helicopter turns to face the way you push the stick. X swings it round to face you, so your shots drop as bombs onto tanks; press X again to face sideways. Set Facing to "Turn button only" for the original controls below.
  • Original controls: X turns. A quick tap swings the helicopter to face you; from there your shots drop as bombs onto tanks. Hold X to swing all the way round, or press it while facing you with ← or → to face that way.

The enemy

  • Tanks shoot at you when you are on the ground, and at hostages. They can't cross the border fence by your base.
  • Jets appear after your first rescue run and fire missiles and drop bombs. Later, air mines hunt you directly.
  • Each trip home makes the enemy stronger. You have three helicopters (sorties).

Touch and gamepad

On a phone, the round pad is the joystick and the buttons fire and turn. A gamepad's left stick works like the original analogue joystick.

About

Choplifter Evolved is a fan tribute to Choplifter by Dan Gorlin (Brøderbund, 1982, Apple II). It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the original's creators or publishers.

The rules, flight model and enemy behaviour follow the original program, from Quinn Dunki's clean-room reverse engineering (github.com/blondie7575/ChoplifterReverse). The Classic pictures and all sounds are new, drawn and synthesised for this tribute; the Desert look is new painted art.

The original ran as fast as the Apple II could draw each frame; the Speed setting chooses that pace.
